question: Why are evaluations the bottleneck for shipping a GenAI product, more than model choice?
idealAnswerCore: GenAI product quality is non-deterministic and prompt/model/data changes can regress silently, so a reliable eval loop is what lets you ship, compare, and rollback — model choice is secondary once you can measure the job-to-be-done.
idealAnswerFraming: Interviewers want to hear that you treat evals as a product system, not a one-off benchmark run. Lead with: without evals you cannot tell if a new prompt, retriever, or model is actually better for users.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: LLM outputs vary with temperature, context, and retrieval; unit tests on code do not catch 'answers look plausible but are wrong'
Most production failures are task-specific (wrong citation, missed policy, bad JSON) — public leaderboards rarely measure those
Evals unlock comparison: prompt A vs B, GPT vs Claude, RAG k=5 vs k=10, with a decision threshold
They also unlock CI: block merges that drop faithfulness, schema validity, or safety pass-rate
A small, high-quality golden set (50–200 cases) beats a huge noisy benchmark for product decisions
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you convince a PM to invest in evals before adding another model?
What happens to velocity if you only use production thumbs-up as your eval?

question: What is the difference between offline evals, online evals, and human evals for an LLM application?
idealAnswerCore: Offline evals score a frozen dataset before deploy; online evals measure live user and system metrics after deploy; human evals are periodic labeled reviews that calibrate automated scores — you need all three because they catch different failure modes.
idealAnswerFraming: Structure the answer as a pipeline: offline as a gate, online as a monitor, human as ground truth. Mention lag, cost, and statistical power of each.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Offline: golden set + automated metrics (exact match, schema validity, LLM-as-judge); cheap, repeatable, no user risk; can overfit the set
Online: task completion, deflection, latency, cost, thumbs, escalation rate; measures real distribution but is noisy and lagged
Human: expert or crowd labels on sampled traces; expensive but required to validate judges and catch novel failures
Use offline to prevent known regressions, online to detect drift and new query types, human to recalibrate
Do not treat online thumbs as a faithfulness metric — users upvote tone as often as correctness
idealAnswerFollowups: When would you skip offline evals and go straight to a canary?
How large does an online experiment need to be to detect a 3% quality drop?

question: How do you build a golden evaluation set for a GenAI feature?
idealAnswerCore: A golden set is a versioned collection of representative inputs with expected properties (reference answers, required citations, must-not-say rules, or rubrics) that you run on every prompt/model/retriever change.
idealAnswerFraming: Emphasize sampling from real traffic, covering failure slices, and keeping labels maintainable. Interviewers ding answers that only say 'use MMLU'.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Start from production traces and support tickets, not synthetic trivia; include easy, typical, and adversarial cases
Stratify by intent, language, document type, risk level, and known failure modes (empty retrieval, conflicting sources)
Label what you can check automatically (JSON schema, citation IDs, refusal) plus a short rubric for open-ended quality
Version the set like code; when product policy changes, update labels rather than silently scoring against stale gold
50 well-labeled cases with error analysis beat 5,000 unlabeled prompts; grow the set from production misses
idealAnswerFollowups: How do you prevent the golden set from leaking into prompt few-shots?
How often should you refresh labels as the product evolves?

question: What should you measure at the component level vs end-to-end in a RAG or agent application?
idealAnswerCore: Component evals isolate retriever, ranker, tool calls, and generator; end-to-end evals score the user-visible answer or task outcome — you debug with components and ship with end-to-end.
idealAnswerFraming: This is the classic 'unit vs integration test' analogy. Show you would not tune chunk size using only thumbs-up, and would not ship using only Recall@k.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Retrieval: Recall@k, MRR, nDCG, hit rate on gold passages
Generation: faithfulness/groundedness, answer relevance, completeness, toxicity
Agents: tool selection accuracy, argument validity, trajectory success, loop/timeout rate
End-to-end: task success, citation correctness, schema validity, latency/cost SLOs
A retrieval win can still be an E2E loss if the generator ignores context ('lost in the middle')
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you attribute an E2E failure to retrieval vs generation?
What component metric would you watch during a vector-index migration?

question: When are deterministic metrics (exact match, F1, BLEU, ROUGE, JSON schema) sufficient, and when do they fail for LLM apps?
idealAnswerCore: Deterministic metrics work when the output is constrained (classification, extraction, SQL, JSON, citations); they fail for open-ended answers where many phrasings are correct and n-gram overlap rewards verbosity or punishes valid paraphrases.
idealAnswerFraming: Show judgment: start with cheap checks as CI gates, then add semantic or judge metrics only where needed.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Great fits: structured extraction, tool-call JSON, regex policy, must-include facts, citation IDs
BLEU/ROUGE correlate poorly with helpfulness for chat; they punish concise correct answers
Exact match is brittle to punctuation, ordering, and equivalent SQL
Combine: schema valid AND key facts present AND judge score for remaining quality
Never let a fluency metric be the only ship gate for factual products
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you score a SQL-generation feature without executing the query?
Why might ROUGE go up while user trust goes down?

question: How does LLM-as-judge evaluation work in a production eval harness, and what biases must you control?
idealAnswerCore: LLM-as-judge prompts a strong model with a rubric (and optionally a reference) to score or rank outputs; it scales cheaper than humans but inherits verbosity, position, self-preference, and scale-calibration biases that you mitigate with swap tests, rubrics, and human calibration.
idealAnswerFraming: Assume the interviewer has heard of LLM-as-judge. Go deeper: pairwise vs pointwise, judge model choice, and how you detect that the judge is gaming itself.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Pointwise: score 1–5 against a rubric; pairwise: choose A vs B (often more stable for ranking changes)
Mitigations: swap position and average, hide model names, use a different judge family than the candidate
Require structured judge output (score + evidence span) so you can audit false convictions
Calibrate against a human-labeled subset; report judge–human agreement (kappa/correlation), not only mean score
Pin judge model/version; a silent judge upgrade can look like a product regression or win
idealAnswerFollowups: When would you prefer a small specialized classifier over a frontier judge?
How do you stop the candidate model from writing 'judge bait' that inflates scores?

question: What is G-Eval and how does it differ from a naive 'rate this 1-5' judge prompt?
idealAnswerCore: G-Eval (Liu et al.) uses chain-of-thought scoring against explicit criteria, often with form-filling and probability-weighted scores, to make LLM judges more aligned with human ratings than a single unconstrained score.
idealAnswerFraming: Name the paper-level idea without being pedantic: structured criteria + reasoning + aggregation beat a vibe score.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Define criteria (coherence, faithfulness, fluency) separately rather than one overall vibe
Ask the judge to reason, then emit a score; optionally weight token probabilities of score tokens
Reduces some noise vs. a one-shot integer, but still needs human calibration
Cost/latency is higher than a tiny classifier — batch offline, not on every live request unless necessary
Pair with deterministic checks so the judge is not the only gate
idealAnswerFollowups: Would you run G-Eval online on 100% of traffic? Why or why not?
How do you version criteria when product policy changes?

question: How do RAGAS-style metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision/recall) map to product decisions?
idealAnswerCore: RAGAS decomposes RAG quality into retrieval and generation axes so you can decide whether to fix the index, the prompt, or the model — faithfulness dropping with stable context recall points at the generator; the reverse points at retrieval.
idealAnswerFraming: Walk through a debugging tree. Interviewers love 'metric → action'.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Faithfulness: claims supported by retrieved context — low means hallucination or ignored context
Answer relevance: addresses the user question — low means off-topic or incomplete even if grounded
Context recall: gold facts appeared in retrieved chunks — low means chunking/index/query issues
Context precision: retrieved chunks are actually useful — low means noisy k or bad ranking
Do not optimize RAGAS blindly: a judge can mark hedging as unfaithful; spot-check disagreements
idealAnswerFollowups: If faithfulness is high but users still complain, what else could be wrong?
How do you compute context recall without gold passages?

question: How do you put LLM evals into CI/CD so prompt and model changes cannot silently regress?
idealAnswerCore: Treat prompts, tools, and retrieval configs as code: on every PR, run a fast eval subset as a gate and a larger suite nightly, fail the build on statistically meaningful drops in contract metrics, and store traces for failed cases.
idealAnswerFraming: Connect this to software engineering: fixtures, flakes, and flake quarantine. Mention cost control so CI does not bankrupt you.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Split suites: smoke (schema, refusals, 20 critical cases) vs full (golden set + judges)
Pin models, judge versions, and temperature; record git SHA of prompts/templates
Define contract metrics (e.g. JSON validity ≥ 99%, faithfulness ≥ 0.85, P95 latency SLO)
Budget: cache embeddings, use cheaper models for smoke, sample traces rather than 100% judge
On failure, dump the worst cases into review — a red number without examples is unusable
idealAnswerFollowups: How do you handle an eval that flakes because the judge is non-deterministic?
Should a 1% drop in a vanity metric block a security fix?

question: How do you detect whether a quality score change is real versus noise?
idealAnswerCore: Treat eval scores as experiments: use paired tests on the same cases, report confidence intervals, and require a minimum effect size plus case-level error analysis before declaring a win.
idealAnswerFraming: This separates senior candidates. Mention McNemar/bootstrap/paired t and the danger of peeking at 30 examples.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Always compare on the same frozen set; shuffling or adding cases mid-experiment confounds results
For binary pass/fail, use paired tests (McNemar); for scores, bootstrap the mean difference
LLM judges add extra variance — run swap tests or average two judge passes if the delta is small
Look at slices: an overall +2% can hide a −15% on a high-risk subset
Never ship on a leaderboard bump without reading failures that flipped
idealAnswerFollowups: How many examples do you need to detect a 5% absolute drop in pass rate?
What is peeking and why does it inflate false wins?

question: What is eval-driven development for GenAI, and how does it differ from demo-driven development?
idealAnswerCore: Eval-driven development writes the failure cases and metrics first, then changes prompts/models until the suite improves without breaking contracts — demo-driven development cherry-picks impressive outputs and discovers regressions in production.
idealAnswerFraming: Frame it as TDD for non-deterministic systems. Mention that evals must include 'do not' cases, not only happy paths.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Capture each production bug as a golden case with an assertion or rubric
Define done as metric movement on slices that matter to the business, not a single viral demo
Include safety and schema contracts alongside helpfulness so you cannot 'win' by being reckless
Review diffs of outputs, not only aggregate scores
Resist adding few-shot examples copied from the eval set — that is overfitting, not learning
idealAnswerFollowups: How do you keep the team from overfitting prompts to the golden set?
Where do product analytics fit in this loop?

question: How should you evaluate tool-using agents differently from single-shot chat completions?
idealAnswerCore: Agent evals must score the trajectory, not only the final string: correct tool choice, valid arguments, termination, side-effect safety, and task success under timeouts — a fluent final answer can hide a dangerous or looping tool path.
idealAnswerFraming: Use a travel-booking or refund example. Interviewers want tool correctness and process metrics.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Process metrics: tool precision/recall, argument schema validity, steps-to-success, retry loops
Outcome metrics: task success, user-visible correctness, cost/tokens, wall-clock
Safety: unauthorized tool calls, writes without confirmation, leaking secrets into tools
Use simulated tools with fixtures so evals are deterministic and cheap
Grade partial credit: right retrieval but failed write vs. hallucinated success
idealAnswerFollowups: How do you eval an agent whose tools hit live APIs?
What is a 'reward hack' in an agent eval?

question: What online product metrics complement model-quality evals for a GenAI application?
idealAnswerCore: Online metrics capture whether the feature actually helps users: task completion, time-to-resolution, deflection, edit distance on suggested text, escalation to humans, retention, and cost per successful task — they complement but do not replace groundedness evals.
idealAnswerFraming: Show you can talk to PMs. Warn against optimizing thumbs at the expense of truthfulness.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Leading indicators: empty-state rate, regenerate clicks, copy/insert rate, follow-up 'that's wrong'
Lagging: CSAT, retention, ticket volume, containment rate for support bots
Operational: P95 TTFT, error rate, $ per session, cache hit rate
Join traces to tickets: a quality drop often shows up in support before in thumbs
Instrument the action (accepted suggestion) not just the impression (shown suggestion)
idealAnswerFollowups: Which online metric would you pick as the north star for an internal coding assistant?
How do you attribute a metric move to a prompt change vs. a traffic mix shift?

question: How do you use production traces as a living eval set without leaking private data or overfitting?
idealAnswerCore: Sample traces, redact PII, cluster by intent, label a stratified subset, and promote only durable cases into the golden set — rotate examples and keep a holdout cluster that prompts never see.
idealAnswerFraming: This is how real teams keep evals representative. Mention privacy and consent.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Continuous sampling with rate limits; overweight failures and low-confidence cases
Redact secrets, customer names, and unique identifiers before labeling or sending to a judge vendor
Cluster embeddings of queries so you do not label 200 duplicates of the same intent
Holdout: never put holdout text into system prompts or few-shots
Expire cases when the product behavior is supposed to change
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you handle traces that contain credentials accidentally pasted by users?
What sampling rate is reasonable for a 10M-request/day assistant?

question: How do you evaluate faithfulness and citation quality when the model can paraphrase retrieved context?
idealAnswerCore: Require atomic claims, check each claim against retrieved passages (NLI/judge/entailment), and score citations at claim-level rather than 'a source was attached somewhere' — paraphrase is allowed; unsupported numbers, names, and policies are not.
idealAnswerFraming: Senior bar: claim decomposition + evidence. Mention that string overlap is insufficient.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Decompose the answer into claims; mark each as supported, contradicted, or not in context
Citation precision: cited chunk actually supports the claim; citation recall: claims that need sources have them
Numeric and named-entity checks are high-ROI automated filters
Allow paraphrase and synthesis across chunks but fail on merged facts that no single or combined source states
Human spot-check legal/medical claims even if the judge is green
idealAnswerFollowups: How do you treat a correct answer that used parametric knowledge not in the retrieved docs?
Would you fail an answer that cites a relevant doc but slightly misquotes a number?

question: What is benchmark contamination and how does it distort both public leaderboards and internal evals?
idealAnswerCore: Contamination is when eval items (or close paraphrases) appeared in pretraining, fine-tuning, or your few-shot prompts, inflating scores without real generalization — it affects MMLU-style benches and also your golden set if you paste eval cases into prompts.
idealAnswerFraming: Show practical defenses: canaries, paraphrase sets, and never training on the eval split.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Public benches leak into internet-scale crawls; a 90% MMLU may not mean your app is accurate
Internal contamination: engineers copy failing evals into the prompt until the suite is green
Detect: n-gram overlap, membership tests, or a secret canary item that should remain unknown
Mitigate: holdout sets, continually refreshed live tasks, execution-based evals (code/SQL)
Report contamination-aware results when claiming SOTA internally
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you design an eval that is hard to contaminate?
Is it contamination if the model saw the policy doc that the answer should cite?

question: How would you design an eval program for a multi-step customer-support agent that can refund, retrieve orders, and escalate?
idealAnswerCore: Build a scenario catalog with fixtures for tools, score both policy compliance and customer outcome, include adversarial and ambiguous tickets, and gate autonomy (refunds) on a higher bar than chat-only answers.
idealAnswerFraming: This is a system-design eval question. Structure: scenarios → simulators → metrics → human review → online holdouts.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Scenarios: happy path, missing order, policy edge (out of window), angry user, injection in ticket text
Simulated tools with deterministic order/refund APIs and injected faults (timeouts, 409s)
Metrics: correct tool sequence, refund amount accuracy, escalation precision/recall, tone, leakage of PII
Separate 'can chat' vs 'can spend money' evals; require human review until refund accuracy is proven
Online: shadow mode (agent proposes, human acts) then canary percent of live tickets
idealAnswerFollowups: How do you eval empathy without letting it override policy?
What fixture design prevents the agent from memorizing order IDs?

question: How do you choose between reference-based, reference-free, and pairwise evaluation?
idealAnswerCore: Use reference-based when a gold answer exists and variation is limited; reference-free (rubric/judge/classifiers) when many answers are valid; pairwise when you are choosing between two systems and relative ranking is more stable than absolute scores.
idealAnswerFraming: Give a decision table. Mention cost and label burden.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Reference-based: extraction, classification, constrained generation; cheap and auditable
Reference-free: open chat, summarization without a single gold; needs strong rubrics
Pairwise: prompt or model bake-offs; reduce position bias with swaps
Hybrid: reference checks for must-have facts + pairwise for style
If you cannot write a rubric an expert agrees on, you are not ready to automate the judge
idealAnswerFollowups: Why might pairwise say A>B while your north-star online metric disagrees?
When is a learned reward model better than a prompted judge?

question: What is slice-based evaluation and why can an overall score hide a launch-blocking failure?
idealAnswerCore: Slice-based evals report metrics on subpopulations (language, tenant, query type, document recency, safety category) so a strong average cannot hide a catastrophic slice — launch decisions should use worst-slice gates for high-risk groups.
idealAnswerFraming: Use an example: English accuracy 92% while Spanish legal queries are 40% hallucinated.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Define slices from product risk, not only from convenience (do not only slice by model version)
Minimum n per slice; merge rare slices rather than reporting noisy 3-example means
Gate on critical slices (safety, billing, medical) even if overall looks fine
Watch mix shift: a metric can rise because easy queries increased, not because the model improved
Dashboards should show slice trends over time, not a single global RAGAS number
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you slice a multi-tenant RAG system?
What do you do when a slice is too small for statistical confidence but legally important?

question: How should evaluation cost and latency be budgeted in a GenAI platform team?
idealAnswerCore: Separate always-on cheap contracts (schema, toxicity classifier, retrieval hit) from sampled expensive judges; cap judge tokens, batch offline, and treat eval spend as a percentage of serving spend so quality measurement stays affordable as traffic grows.
idealAnswerFraming: Senior platform answer: unit economics of evals. Mention caching embeddings and reusing traces.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Budget heuristic: eval spend often 5–20% of inference during active development, less in steady state
Cascade: regex/schema → small classifier → LLM judge only on uncertain or sampled cases
Cache judge results keyed by (prompt_hash, model, input_hash) for unchanged cases
Nightly full suite vs PR smoke suite to keep developer latency low
If evals are too expensive, teams skip them — cheaper evals that run beat perfect evals that do not
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you eval a 100k-request/hour system with a frontier judge?
When is it worth paying for human labels instead of more judge calls?

question: What is the difference between model-centric benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, MT-Bench) and application evals?
idealAnswerCore: Model-centric benchmarks compare general capabilities of foundation models; application evals measure whether your product completes a specific job on your data, policies, and UX constraints — a model can win MT-Bench and still fail your invoice-extraction SLA.
idealAnswerFraming: Clear this confusion early in interviews. Application evals are the ones you own.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval: research comparability, contamination risk, weak product correlation
MT-Bench/Arena: preference for chat style, not factuality on your corpus
Application evals: your schemas, your docs, your refusal policy, your latency budget
Use public benches to shortlist models; use application evals to select and ship
Never tell leadership 'we are GPT-4 level' based only on a public leaderboard
idealAnswerFollowups: When is a public benchmark still useful in a product meeting?
How do you eval a model upgrade with both types?

question: What are contract tests for LLM outputs, and why should they run before any judge?
idealAnswerCore: Contract tests are cheap, deterministic assertions — JSON schema, required fields, PII patterns, forbidden phrases, citation format, language, length — that fail fast in CI and production without a judge.
idealAnswerFraming: Analogize to API contract tests. Judges are slow and fuzzy; contracts are the first safety net.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Examples: valid JSON, enum values, SQL parseable, markdown table shape, no raw stack traces
Safety contracts: no system-prompt leak markers, no secret-shaped strings, refusal on disallowed intents
Run on 100% of outputs in prod as well as in evals — they are both tests and guardrails
Keep contracts versioned with the product spec
If a contract is flaky, it is too vague — tighten it rather than adding a judge
idealAnswerFollowups: What contract would you write for a citations-required RAG answer?
How do contracts interact with streaming tokens?

question: How do you evaluate summarization quality for long documents in a business setting?
idealAnswerCore: Combine coverage of required entities/decisions, faithfulness to source, length/format constraints, and task usefulness (can a human act on it) — not ROUGE alone — and grade with source-grounded claim checks plus a small expert review panel.
idealAnswerFraming: Use meeting notes or legal discovery as the example. Mention that abstractive summaries hallucinate entities.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Check must-include items (action items, amounts, parties) with entity-level recall
Faithfulness via claim-to-source alignment; fail on invented commitments
Format contracts: bullets, max length, audience (exec vs engineer)
Pairwise preference only after factual checks pass
Expert reviewers for a sampled set; domain jargon is where judges fail
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you eval a summary of a 200-page PDF that does not fit in context?
What failure is worse: omission or hallucination in an exec summary?

question: What is a teacher/student or cheaper-model proxy eval, and when is it dangerous?
idealAnswerCore: A cheaper model or distilled judge estimates quality at high volume; it is useful for smoke tests and trend detection but dangerous if it disagrees systematically with experts on the cases that matter (safety, numbers, rare languages).
idealAnswerFraming: Show you would calibrate and monitor disagreement, not blindly trust the cheap judge.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Train or prompt a small grader on human-labeled traces
Use it for PR smoke and sampling; periodically re-label against humans/frontier judges
Danger: the proxy shares weaknesses with the candidate (both miss the same legal nuance)
Keep a gold panel the proxy never trains on
Watch score inflation as you optimize against the proxy (Goodhart's law)
idealAnswerFollowups: How is this different from using the same model as generator and judge?
What is Goodhart's law in eval design?

question: How do you evaluate multimodal GenAI (images, PDFs, screenshots) beyond text-only metrics?
idealAnswerCore: Eval both perception (did the model read the chart/table/UI correctly?) and generation (is the answer grounded in the visual evidence?), using labeled regions, OCR/table gold, and visual QA cases — plus the same safety contracts as text.
idealAnswerFraming: Call out that text judges cannot see the image unless you pass it to a multimodal judge.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Gold: key numbers from charts, checkbox states, table cells, UI labels
Use multimodal judges or specialized extractors; do not describe the image in text and then grade that description only
Include degraded inputs: blurry scans, rotated pages, tiny fonts
Measure grounding: the answer should refer to visible evidence, not invent UI that is not there
Safety: refuse disallowed visual content; do not extract PII from IDs unless allowed
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you eval a 'screenshot to ticket' assistant?
What unique hallucination modes do vision-language models have?

question: What role do inter-rater reliability and rubrics play in human evaluation?
idealAnswerCore: Human eval is only trustworthy if raters share a rubric and you measure agreement (Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa, gold-standard audits); without that, score changes may be rater drift, not model change.
idealAnswerFraming: Interviewers use this to see if you have run a real labeling program.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Write a rubric with examples of 1 vs 5, including borderline cases
Train raters and include hidden gold items to detect fatigue and bias
Double-label a subset; investigate systematic disagreements (often rubric holes)
Separate dimensions (correctness vs tone) so raters do not mix them
Pay for expertise on high-stakes domains rather than only cheap crowd ratings
idealAnswerFollowups: What kappa would you consider acceptable for a 5-point helpfulness scale?
How do you handle a task where even experts disagree?

question: How would you run a model or prompt bake-off for a production RAG assistant without wrecking the live user experience?
idealAnswerCore: Use offline golden + shadow traffic (log what the candidate would have said) then a small canary with paired online metrics and kill criteria — never A/B 50% until offline contracts pass and shadow disagreement is understood.
idealAnswerFraming: Sequence: offline gate → shadow → canary → ramp. Mention cost of double inference.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Offline: same retrieval snapshot so you isolate generator/prompt effects when needed
Shadow: run candidate on sampled live queries, store diffs, judge or human-review disagreements
Canary: 1–5% traffic, watch safety, latency, cost, and task metrics; auto-rollback on SLO breach
Control mix: sticky assignment so a user does not bounce between prompts mid-session
Document residual risks the evals cannot see (new doc types) as launch notes
idealAnswerFollowups: How do you shadow an agent that has side-effecting tools?
What kill criteria would you set for a canary?

question: What is error analysis in LLM evals and how should it feed the roadmap?
idealAnswerCore: Error analysis is a structured review of failures grouped into a taxonomy (retrieval miss, ignored context, tool error, policy miss, format break) with frequency and severity — the top buckets become prompt, data, or product work, not a generic 'make the model smarter'.
idealAnswerFraming: This is how evals become engineering tickets. Show a taxonomy.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Tag each failure with a primary cause; allow secondary tags
Plot volume × severity; fix high-severity rare events (wrong refund) before low-severity nits
Feed new tags back as slices and golden cases
Distinguish 'model cannot' vs 'we did not give the tool/docs' vs 'policy unclear'
Re-run analysis after each major change to confirm the bucket actually moved
idealAnswerFollowups: How large a sample do you need for a useful taxonomy?
What if 40% of errors are 'user asked something out of scope'?

question: Why is a single 'accuracy' number a poor summary of GenAI quality?
idealAnswerCore: GenAI quality is multi-objective — correctness, grounding, safety, latency, cost, and UX — and accuracy usually hides the dimension that will cause the incident; report a small scorecard with contracts, not one vanity percentage.
idealAnswerFraming: Push back on executives asking for one number, then offer a dashboard they can use.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: A model can be accurate in tone and wrong on facts, or vice versa
Safety and helpfulness trade off; collapsing them invites reward hacking
Latency/cost are part of quality for interactive products
Present: pass-rate on contracts, faithfulness, safety, P95 latency, $ / success
Use one north-star for product (e.g. successful resolutions) but never as the only eval
idealAnswerFollowups: Which three numbers would you put on a weekly GenAI quality email?
How do you explain a quality drop that improved safety?

question: How do you keep judges and reward models from being Goodharted as teams optimize against them?
idealAnswerCore: Assume any metric used as a target will be gamed: rotate holdouts, mix human audits, keep multiple weakly correlated metrics, and change the judge/rubric periodically so prompt hacking the grader is unprofitable.
idealAnswerFraming: Name Goodhart/Campbell's law. Give concrete gaming examples (verbose answers, fake citations).
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Teams add 'as cited in the documentation' without real citations if judges reward that phrase
Use hidden holdout cases and live traffic samples the prompt authors do not see
Require evidence spans from judges; spot-check high scores
Optimize under constraints (length, citation precision) not a single scalar
Periodic human panels reset the target when automated scores decouple from trust
idealAnswerFollowups: How is this different from overfitting a golden set?
Would you show eval scores on a public leaderboard internally?
